A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites so people can load pages faster. Normally, every request for a page travels back to one origin server, meaning the original computer where the website's files live. If that computer is far away, loading takes longer. A content delivery network solves this by placing copies of the website on servers closer to visitors, called edge locations, since they sit near the "edge" of the network, closer to homes and offices rather than in one distant data center. When someone requests a page and a nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to serve, that's called a cache hit, and it means the page arrives almost instantly without needing to contact the distant origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries keeping popular books on local shelves instead of forcing every reader to travel to one central national library. If a nearby shelf has the book already, it gets handed over immediately; if not, the local library requests it from the central one, keeps a copy, and hands it over sooner next time. This is why streaming video, online shopping, and news sites feel fast almost everywhere: nearby copies handle most requests, while the original source is only contacted occasionally.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | It's the ultimate source, but slow if used for every request |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding a copy of the content | Cuts distance, making pages load faster |
| Cache hit | A request answered by a nearby saved copy | Saves time by avoiding a trip to the origin server |
| Content delivery network | The whole system of edge locations working together | Keeps websites fast and reliable for people everywhere |
